context.text: Incumbent Lizzie Pannill Fletcher (D) ran unopposed in the March 3, 2026 Democratic primary. Alexander Hale won a May 26, 2026 Republican primary runoff against Tina Blum Cohen, 64.3% to 35.7%. As of September 2026, forecasters (Cook Political Report, Decision Desk HQ, Inside Elections, Sabato's Crystal Ball) rated the general election Solid/Safe Democratic.

candidates.name: Lizzie Pannill Fletcher

summary.text: Lizzie Pannill Fletcher is the Democratic incumbent U.S. Representative for Texas's 7th Congressional District, a Houston lawyer.

background.text: Born and raised in Houston, Texas; graduated from St. John's School, earned a bachelor's degree in history from Kenyon College, and a J.D. from William & Mary Law School.
Worked as a lawyer before being elected to Congress; co-founded Planned Parenthood Young Leaders in 2000.
Serves as a board member of Writers in the Schools and the Open Dance Project.

positions.summary: In a June 2026 press release, said she voted against a $70 billion DHS funding bill that included $38.5 billion for ICE because it included no reforms or accountability, and said she introduced a bill to freeze ICE hiring.
positions.quote: This legislation, however, includes zero reforms and no accountability.

positions.summary: In a July 2022 press release, said she voted to reinstate the federal assault weapons ban and supports it as a way to make communities safer.
positions.quote: Passing the Assault Weapons Ban and keeping these weapons of war off our streets is one way Congress can help make our communities safer.

record.text: Serves on the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, including the Health Subcommittee and the Oversight and Investigations Subcommittee, in the 2025–2026 Congress.

candidates.researchNotes: Positions are drawn from official-site press releases (immigration, 2026; guns, 2022); issue pages on fletcher.house.gov carry only links to press releases. No Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey was found.

candidates.name: Alexander Hale
candidates.ballotNote: Won the May 26, 2026 Republican primary runoff against Tina Blum Cohen

summary.text: Alexander Hale is the Republican nominee for Texas's 7th Congressional District.

background.text: Energy and chemicals consultant at Alvarez & Marsal; previously worked at AEI, in the U.S. Senate and at Patriot Capital (as described in his Community Impact candidate profile).

priorities.text: Houston's energy economy: defend Houston's role in the energy industry.
priorities.quote: Defend Houston's role as the energy capital of America.

priorities.text: Affordability and fiscal responsibility, starting with federal deficit spending.
priorities.quote: Affordability and Fiscal Responsibility: fix what's driving prices up in the first place, starting with Washington's wasteful deficit spending.

priorities.text: Healthcare costs: price transparency and competition.
priorities.quote: Healthcare: lower costs through price transparency and real competition, not more middlemen.

positions.summary: Says he will fight to restore full Byrne JAG federal grant funding for local law enforcement, and lists funding law enforcement among his priorities.
positions.quote: Alexander will fight to restore full Byrne JAG funding and oppose any effort to condition those grants on the adoption of progressive policing mandates dressed up as reform.

candidates.researchNotes: Found halefortexas.com priority pages, a Community Impact Q&A (Aug. 28, 2026) and the Ballotpedia-quoted Feb. 2026 version of his site. The school choice and border statements come from that earlier site text, which has since been replaced by the current priority pages. No Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey. Positions on abortion, guns, taxes and tariffs not found.

statements.quote: Build more, faster. Cut the federal red tape that makes it more expensive to build a house, a power plant, or a pipeline in Houston.
statements.context: On the Affordability page of his campaign site

statements.quote: Let families pay their doctor directly with pre-tax dollars, and keep insurance for real emergencies.
statements.context: On the Healthcare page of his campaign site

statements.quote: Champion an all-of-the-above strategy: oil, gas, nuclear, refining, and innovation.
statements.context: On the Energy page of his campaign site

statements.quote: School choice and innovative approaches are key to improving student outcomes within the district.
statements.context: On his campaign website, as quoted by Ballotpedia on Feb. 20, 2026

statements.quote: We must continue to secure our border and counter the negative effects of illegal entry.
statements.context: On his campaign website, as quoted by Ballotpedia on Feb. 20, 2026

candidates.name: Espoir Ngabo
candidates.ballotNote: Won the Green Party convention nomination

summary.text: Espoir Ngabo is an information-technology professional running as the Green Party nominee for Texas's 7th Congressional District on a platform funded with no corporate money.

background.text: Built a nearly decade-long career in information technology, supporting business systems and infrastructure.
Based in Houston and connected to the Alief, Sharpstown, and Gulfton communities.

priorities.text: Says his campaign takes zero corporate money and is "powered by everyday people."
Calls for stronger flood protection and disaster preparedness, reliable public transit, and safer roads and sidewalks in the district.

positions.summary: Supports a $25 federal minimum wage indexed to the cost of living.
positions.quote: a $25 federal minimum wage that keeps up with the cost of living

positions.summary: Supports a single-payer healthcare system covering everyone.
positions.quote: healthcare for everyone through a single-payer system

statements.quote: billionaires should pay their fair share instead of gaming the system while working families get squeezed.
statements.context: In his Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey (Sept. 23, 2026)

candidates.researchNotes: Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey (May and Sept. 2026) and a Community Impact Q&A (Aug. 28, 2026) reviewed. Housing, flood, transit and campaign-finance proposals he lists do not map directly to the guide's issues. No abortion, guns, immigration, tax-rate or climate positions found beyond the statement shown.
